title: She Spoke Up for Women's Rights and Was Executed for Treason
dek: Olympe de Gouges is known for the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but she was killed not for her feminist arguments — she was killed for opposing the king's execution and attacking Robespierre.
why: To understand women's political position and one individual's fate during the French Revolution. History buffs and people following women's-rights issues will be interested.
who: Anyone interested in the French Revolution, women's history, or women's writing during the Enlightenment — especially readers who want the details of women's political participation that textbooks leave out.
skip: The first four-plus minutes, on the many ambiguities of her early life, can be fast-forwarded; the core material starts in the middle.

points.h: The Declaration of the Rights of Woman answers the Declaration of the Rights of Man
points.body: Olympe de Gouges is most famous for the 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she switched to the feminine form citoyenne — it looks completely different but sounds nearly the same. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this one pamphlet, and her death sentence was not for calling for women's rights.

points.h: Biographical truth is mixed with novelistic invention
points.body: The first English biography of de Gouges, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, draws heavily on her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but the book is highly fictional. Its protagonist is widely considered a stand-in for herself, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. That parentage has never been confirmed.

points.h: The Comédie-Française crushed a woman playwright
points.body: Zamore and Mirza was written in 1784 and submitted anonymously; it was accepted the following year but its staging was long delayed. When de Gouges kept pressing, the theater actually revoked her right of entry and applied for her arrest. Between 1761 and 1789 the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only author treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her position.

points.h: Slavery became the first abolitionist play
points.body: The play finally opened in 1789, but its setting moved from the East Indies to the Caribbean, its characters changed from Asians to Africans, and its title became Slavery of the Blacks. It is often regarded as France's first play to explicitly support abolition and to tell the story from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy men with colonial interests hired hecklers to disrupt it, and the actors refused to blacken their skin for the roles.

points.h: The article rewrites all 17 articles one by one
points.body: The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted rights to citizens but excluded women, and the 1791 constitution restricted the vote to taxpaying men. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the 17-article format and rewrote each article in turn. Where the original's Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, for instance, she added that a mother has the right to publicly declare the father of her child. The whole document was dedicated to Marie Antoinette, urging her to advance women's rights.

points.h: Defending Louis XVI became the rope around her neck
points.body: Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed a constitutional monarchy suited France best, with the king as a symbol rather than a holder of power. At Louis XVI's treason trial in 1792 she volunteered to defend him, on the grounds that the monarchy had already been abolished and a republic could not try a former king for acts committed while he reigned. Her logic was called strained; the king was executed anyway, and she was seen as a royalist.

points.h: Her federalist proposal led to her arrest
points.body: In July 1793, de Gouges proposed that France's provinces govern themselves rather than form a unified republic, which was seen as a direct provocation. She underestimated the ferocious political atmosphere of the Terror, and brought investigators to her office herself, thinking her work would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Saved was used as evidence against her for sympathizing with Marie Antoinette. She was ultimately executed for opposing the republican constitution.

terms.def: The French masculine noun meaning a male citizen. De Gouges used citoyenne, its feminine form.
